title: Comparative analysis of YOLO architectures for automated casting defect detection in industrial quality control

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The global casting industry, valued at USD 145.2 billion in 2023, underpins manufacturing sectors including automotive, aerospace, and industrial machinery [ 1 ]. Quality control represents both a significant operational challenge and a competitive differentiator, with defect-related costs accounting for 5–12% of total production expenses in typical foundry operations [ 2 ]. Casting defects arise from complex interactions among process parameters, material properties, and environmental conditions during solidification [ 3 ].

Traditional manual inspection methods remain prevalent globally, with an estimated 68% of foundries relying primarily on human inspection. This figure varies considerably by region: higher automation adoption has been reported in Western Europe and Japan (approximately 45–50% manual reliance) compared with emerging manufacturing economies in South and Southeast Asia (approximately 75–85%) [ 4 ]. These manual systems suffer from well-documented limitations: inspector fatigue leads to a 23% detection rate degradation over 8-hour shifts; subjective interpretation introduces 15–20% inter-operator variability; and throughput constraints limit inspection to 5–10% of total production volume [ 4 ].

Despite the proliferation of deep learning in manufacturing, several critical gaps persist in the literature: (1) To the best of the authors’ knowledge  no systematic comparison of modern YOLO variants specifically for casting defect detection has been reported; (2) previous casting studies have focused on image classification without the spatial localisation required for automated defect remediation; (3) only 23% of published studies include rigorous statistical validation of reported performance differences [ 5 ]; and (4) limited reporting of inference speed, model size, and deployment requirements hinders practical industrial implementation. This study addresses these gaps through a comprehensive evaluation of YOLOv5s, YOLOv8s, and YOLO11s on a real-world industrial pump impeller dataset, extending beyond accuracy metrics to encompass inference speed, computational efficiency, statistical reliability, and Industry 4.0 deployment considerations including MES integration and edge computing requirements [ 6 ,  7 ].

The primary contributions of this work are:  A systematic comparison of three modern YOLO variants for casting defect detection, with publicly available training scripts and image subset list to support reproducibility; Establishment of performance benchmarks achieving 99.9% precision at 196 FPS inference on standard industrial GPU hardware; A bootstrap-based statistical validation framework providing 95% confidence intervals and permutation tests suitable for single-run model comparisons; A learning curve analysis identifying the annotation saturation threshold for binary casting inspection; and Practical deployment guidelines, including an architecture selection matrix, bridging experimental results and industrial implementation.

sections.heading: Deep learning for industrial defect detection
paragraphs: Computer vision systems for industrial quality control have evolved through three broadly defined generations. First-generation systems (1990–2005) employed rule-based image processing, achieving 70–80% detection accuracy under controlled conditions [ 8 ]. Second-generation approaches (2005–2015) introduced machine learning classifiers, improving accuracy to 85–90%; Support Vector Machines, for example, achieved 88% accuracy on casting defects when combined with hand-crafted features [ 9 ]. The current generation, enabled by deep learning, demonstrates accuracy exceeding 95% while automating feature extraction [ 10 ]. Early CNN applications achieved 92% classification accuracy on casting defects but required pre-segmented defect regions [ 11 ]. Region-based CNNs improved detection to 94% mAP but required approximately 2.3 s per image, which is incompatible with real-time production inspection [ 12 ].

sections.heading: YOLO architectures in manufacturing inspection
paragraphs: Within deep learning, YOLO architectures have emerged as well-suited for industrial deployment owing to their single-stage detection pipeline, which enables real-time processing at high throughput [ 13 ]. Recent applications span diverse inspection domains: Chen et al. [ 14 ] integrated RevCol with YOLOv8s for magnetic block surface defect detection; Yu et al. [ 15 ] proposed an improved YOLOv8-based method for concrete surface crack detection; Wang et al. achieved 89 FPS with 93% mAP on fabric defect detection [ 16 ]; Sekhar et al. [ 17 ] identified welding defects with 95% accuracy at 112 FPS; Huang et al. [ 18 ] achieved 96.8% mAP on solar panel defects with a 23% reduction in inference time relative to YOLOv5; and Long and Lin [ 19 ] achieved a 4.4% mAP improvement while reducing parameters by 61.1% via YOLOv8x-ECW for fiberboard surface defect detection. In the casting domain, Sani et al. reported 99.45% balanced accuracy in pump impeller classification using transfer learning, though without the spatial localisation required for automated robotic rejection [ 20 ].

Collectively, these studies demonstrate the versatility of YOLO architectures across inspection modalities. However, no published work has systematically compared YOLOv5s, YOLOv8s, and YOLO11s specifically for casting defect detection, nor do existing studies consistently report the deployment metrics—inference latency, model size, and energy consumption—necessary for informed industrial implementation decisions. The present study addresses this gap.

sections.heading: Manufacturing environment and data acquisition
Defect taxonomy and binary classification rationale
paragraphs: The dataset encompasses seven defect categories with distinct formation mechanisms: (i) blow holes from gas entrapment during solidification; (ii) pinholes indicating microporosity that compromises surface integrity; (iii) burr formations from mould parting line flash; (iv) shrinkage cavities from inadequate feeding systems; (v) mould material inclusions causing stress concentrations; (vi) cold shuts from incomplete fusion of metal streams; and (vii) metallurgical defects including grain boundary segregation.

sections.heading: Dataset preparation
paragraphs: From the complete dataset of 7340 images, a representative subset of 1300 images (17.7%) was selected using a strict stratified random sampling protocol applied independently to each class folder ( def_front  and  ok_front ) with a fixed random seed of 42, ensuring reproducibility and eliminating manual selection bias. The resulting subset comprised 781 defective images (60.1%) and 519 non-defective images (39.9%), preserving the class ratio of the full dataset to within rounding precision.

The subset size of 17.7% was further validated empirically through a learning curve analysis presented in Sect.  4.1.3 , which demonstrates that mAP@0.5 saturates at approximately 600–700 training images, placing the full 1170-image training set comfortably within the saturation zone.

sections.heading: Architecture selection criteria
paragraphs: Three YOLO variants were selected to represent evolutionary stages in single-stage object detection, with the “small” (s) variant chosen for each architecture to balance detection performance with the computational constraints of industrial edge devices.

YOLOv5s  (Ultralytics, 2020) serves as the baseline architecture, employing a CSPDarknet53 backbone with 9.1M parameters and 23.8 GFLOPs computation. The architecture’s CSP bottlenecks optimise gradient flow across layers. Despite the absence of a formal peer-reviewed publication, YOLOv5 has achieved widespread industrial adoption and integration into commercial deployment platforms.

YOLOv8s  (Ultralytics, January 2023) introduced three principal refinements: anchor-free detection, eliminating manual anchor configuration; a decoupled head design separating classification and localisation tasks; and C2f modules replacing CSP blocks for enhanced feature fusion. With 11.1M parameters and 28.4 GFLOPs, YOLOv8s increases computation relative to YOLOv5s while delivering improved accuracy through architectural design rather than parameter scaling. Recent studies corroborate its suitability for industrial inspection: Hao et al. [ 23 ] applied an enhanced YOLOv8-based model for hot-rolled steel surface defect detection; Liu et al. [ 24 ] used YOLOv8 for CFRP composite defect detection via nonlinear frequency modulation thermography; and Huang et al. [ 25 ] reported 2.4% and 8.3% improvements in mAP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95, respectively, with a YOLOv8n-based model for wire-arc additive manufacturing inspection.

YOLO11s  (Ultralytics, 2024) incorporates attention mechanisms for enhanced feature discrimination and dynamic label assignment that adapts to the object distribution during training. With 9.4M parameters and optimised computation paths, YOLO11s offers comparable accuracy to YOLOv8s at a lower parameter count. Industrial deployment experience remains limited given its recent release, making a rigorous empirical evaluation of direct relevance to practitioners.

Detection performance metrics
paragraphs: Performance was evaluated using standard object detection metrics. Precision (positive predictive value) quantifies the false alarm rate; recall (sensitivity) measures the defect detection rate; and F1-score provides a balanced summary of the two. Mean Average Precision was evaluated at two IoU thresholds: mAP@0.5 represents standard detection performance and mAP@0.5:0.95 assesses localisation quality, relevant for automated defect measurement applications.

sections.heading: Deployment metrics
paragraphs: Deployment-critical metrics were evaluated under production-representative conditions: single-image inference (batch size 1) with no test-time augmentation, and a confidence threshold of 0.45 optimised on the validation set. Metrics reported include inference latency (ms/image), throughput (FPS), model size (MB), and peak GPU memory. Experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU (16 GB VRAM).

sections.heading: Statistical validation framework
Primary performance metrics
paragraphs: Table  3  summarises the detection performance of the three architectures on the 130-image validation set. YOLOv8s achieved the highest overall performance with 99.9% precision and 100% recall, yielding zero false negatives across the validation set and an mAP@0.5 of 99.5%. YOLOv5s demonstrated robust baseline performance with 96.7% precision, 98.1% recall, and an F1-score of 97.4%, exceeding the accuracy typically reported for manual inspection. The mAP@0.5−0.95 of 93.2% for YOLOv5s suggests slightly reduced localisation precision relative to the other two architectures. YOLO11s achieved intermediate classification performance (98.9% precision, 99.4% recall) while attaining the highest mAP@0.5−0.95 of 94.8%, indicating superior bounding box regression among all three models. Training convergence curves are shown in Fig.  3 . sections.heading: Statistical significance and reliability
paragraphs: Bootstrap resampling (1000 iterations with replacement) of the 130-image validation set was used as the primary measure of result stability. The 95% confidence intervals derived from the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles confirm that the near-perfect performance of YOLOv8s and YOLO11s is stable across hypothetical resampled validation sets. YOLOv8s intervals spanned Precision [0.984−1.000], Recall [0.962−1.000], F1 [0.977−1.000], and mAP@0.5 [0.988−1.000]. YOLO11s produced comparable intervals of Precision [0.971−1.000], Recall [0.954−1.000], F1 [0.968−1.000], and mAP@0.5 [0.981−1.000]. YOLOv5s returned slightly wider intervals—Precision [0.942−0.990], Recall [0.961−0.998], F1 [0.951−0.985], mAP@0.5 [0.962−0.997]—indicating marginally greater performance variability, though remaining within a practically acceptable range.

sections.heading: Learning curve analysis
paragraphs: To validate the 1170-image training subset and characterise performance under constrained annotation budgets, YOLOv8s was trained on five progressively larger subsets (200, 400, 600, 900, and 1170 images) drawn from the same stratified pool, with all evaluations on the fixed 130-image validation set under identical hyperparameters (seed = 42, 80 epochs). Results are shown in Fig.  4  and Table  6 .

The 1170-image training set operated 470–570 images above the saturation threshold. The 0.001 difference between the learning curve result at 1170 images (mAP@0.5 = 0.994) and the main experiment (0.995) reflects normal training stochasticity. For practitioners, approximately 600–700 annotated images represent the minimum for balanced binary casting defect detection with small-variant YOLO architectures on comparable datasets; 1000–1200 images provide saturation-zone reliability. Fig. 4 YOLOv8s learning curve across five training set sizes (200–1170 images) evaluated on a fixed 130-image validation set. The saturation threshold is at approximately 600–700 images. sections.heading: Real-time performance capabilities
paragraphs: Inference consistency, measured as the standard deviation of processing times across 1000 sequential images, remained below 0.3 ms for all architectures, confirming deterministic behaviour suitable for synchronised production line integration. A speed–accuracy trade-off analysis identified Pareto-optimal configurations: YOLOv5s for throughput-critical applications, YOLOv8s for balanced requirements, and YOLO11s for localisation- critical applications where the marginal speed reduction is justified by superior bounding box precision. Fig. 5 Inference speed and detection performance trade-off.   a  shows per-image processing times for YOLOv5s (4.7 ms), YOLOv8s (5.1 ms), and YOLO11s (5.6 ms).   b  plots FPS against mAP@0.5

sections.heading: Scalability and batch processing
paragraphs: Batch processing experiments demonstrated near-linear throughput scaling up to a batch size of 8. At this batch size, throughput reached 1504 FPS (YOLOv5s), 1432 FPS (YOLOv8s), and 1312 FPS (YOLO11s), supporting simultaneous inspection of multiple production streams from a single GPU deployment. Peak GPU memory consumption at batch size 8 was 2.8 GB (YOLOv5s), 3.2 GB (YOLOv8s), and 3.0 GB (YOLO11s), remaining within the capacity of entry-level industrial GPUs (8 GB VRAM) and indicating that multi-stream deployment does not require high-end hardware.

sections.heading: Precision–recall trade-off analysis
paragraphs: The precision–recall curves (Fig.  6 ) revealed distinct operational characteristics across architectures. YOLOv8s maintained precision above 95% across the entire recall range up to 0.98, indicating robust performance across confidence thresholds. The AUC-PR values—0.999 (YOLOv8s), 0.991 (YOLO11s), and 0.974 (YOLOv5s)—quantify the reliability of each model across the full range of operating conditions. Optimal confidence thresholds, determined by F1-score maximisation on the validation set, were 0.42 (YOLOv5s), 0.45 (YOLOv8s), and 0.48 (YOLO11s), achieving false-positive rates below 3.3% while maintaining recall above 98% for all three architectures. Fig. 6 Precision–recall curves for  a  YOLOv5s (mAP@0.5: 0.981),  b  YOLOv8s (mAP@0.5: 0.995), and  c  YOLO11s (mAP@0.5: 0.991). Results shown for defective class (grey), non-defective class (orange), and combined (blue)

sections.heading: Confusion matrix analysis
paragraphs: Confusion matrices normalised across the 130-image validation set (Fig.  7 ) revealed distinct error patterns. YOLOv8s achieved near-perfect classification with one false positive (0.1% FP rate) and zero false negatives. YOLOv5s exhibited 22 false positives and 12 false negatives, indicating a slight tendency toward over-detection. YOLO11s showed intermediate behaviour with seven false positives and four false negatives. The Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC)—which accounts for all four confusion matrix cells and is robust to class imbalance— was 0.999 (YOLOv8s), 0.983 (YOLO11s), and 0.947 (YOLOv5s), consistent with the primary metric results in Table  3 . Fig. 7 Normalised confusion matrices for  a  YOLOv5s,  b  YOLOv8s, and  c  YOLO11s evaluated on 130 validation images. Values indicate proportions normalised by true class frequency

sections.heading: Localisation precision and bounding box quality
Model size and storage requirements
paragraphs: Model footprint metrics relevant to edge deployment are summarised in Table  7 . YOLOv5s required 18.5 MB of storage, YOLOv8s 22.5 MB, and YOLO11s 19.2 MB. All three are substantially smaller than traditional CNN architectures such as VGG16 (528 MB), representing a 95.5% reduction that facilitates deployment on resource-constrained industrial edge devices. Model loading times were 0.82 s (YOLOv5s), 0.94 s (YOLOv8s), and 0.87 s (YOLO11s) on standard industrial PC configurations, all well within typical production line initialisation requirements. sections.heading: Energy consumption and thermal characteristics
paragraphs: Power consumption during continuous inference averaged 42 W (YOLOv5s), 48 W (YOLOv8s), and 45 W (YOLO11s), compared to 15 W at idle. Assuming 24/7 operation at an illustrative industrial electricity rate of USD 0.12/kWh, the estimated annual electricity costs are USD 441 (YOLOv5s), USD 504 (YOLOv8s), and USD 473 (YOLO11s). The inter-architecture difference of USD 63 per annum is negligible relative to hardware and integration costs, confirming that energy consumption should not be a primary criterion for architecture selection.

Peak GPU temperatures under continuous load were 67 °C (YOLOv5s), 71 °C (YOLOv8s), and 69 °C (YOLO11s), remaining within safe operating limits and requiring no specialised cooling beyond standard industrial enclosure ventilation. These thermal profiles are compatible with foundry environments where ambient temperatures typically reach 35–40 °C.

sections.heading: Convergence analysis
paragraphs: Training progression (Fig.  10 ) revealed distinct convergence patterns across architectures. YOLOv8s demonstrated the fastest convergence, reaching 90% of its final mAP@0.5 by epoch 25. YOLOv5s improved steadily through epoch 45 before plateauing. Across all three architectures, stable convergence was reached by approximately epoch 25, with minimal fluctuation thereafter, confirming that the 80-epoch training budget was sufficient and that none of the models showed signs of continued improvement that would justify extended training.

YOLO11s exhibited transient non-monotonic behaviour with a temporary performance dip at epochs 3–4, attributed to the dynamic label assignment strategy requiring initial calibration, before recovering to its final performance level. Despite this early instability, YOLO11s achieved the highest final mAP@0.5−0.95 of 0.948, reflecting superior bounding box regression relative to the other two architectures. sections.heading: Validation loss stability
Ablation study
Architecture selection framework
paragraphs: A staged implementation pathway may reduce operational risk during transition from manual inspection. Phase 1 involves parallel operation alongside manual inspection for a validation period. Phase 2 transitions to automated primary inspection with a statistical sampling overlay. Phase 3 implements full automation with exception-based human intervention. These findings corroborate recent work demonstrating YOLO’s effectiveness in industrial inspection: Li et al. (2025) applied YOLO-LitePV to photovoltaic panel defect detection [ 26 ], and Han et al. (2025) combined YOLOv5 with phased array ultrasonic testing for weld defect recognition [ 27 ], both highlighting the importance of balancing detection accuracy with computational efficiency.

The deployment feasibility of all three architectures is supported by their modest computational footprint: model sizes of 18.5−22.5 MB and energy consumption of 42–48 W enable deployment on standard industrial edge hardware. A comprehensive return-on-investment analysis requires site-specific data on production volume, defect rates, and integration complexity, which are beyond the scope of this study; practitioners are directed to published foundry automation frameworks for site-specific economic evaluation [ 28 ]

sections.heading: Limitations and future work
paragraphs: The evolution of this work follows a three-stage trajectory. In the first stage, enhanced detection capability, multi-view inspection would address non-visible defect surfaces, multi-class defect taxonomy with sub-region annotations would enable discrimination between defect morphologies, and tiled inference on high-resolution inputs would extend sensitivity to sub-2 mm defects. Transfer learning from the current models is expected to require only 200–500 images to adapt to new casting product types. In the second stage, process-aware quality prediction, the detection system would be integrated with real-time casting process data streams (pouring temperature, mould filling speed, cooling rate, metal composition) via OPC UA to correlate defect patterns with upstream process variables, enabling predictive intervention before defects manifest at the inspection station. In the third stage, zero-defect autonomous manufacturing, multi-view detection, multi-class classification, and closed-loop process feedback would be combined into a self-optimising quality system. Federated learning across foundry networks would enable continuous model improvement from distributed production data, supporting convergence toward zero-defect targets aligned with Industry 5.0 objectives.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Statistical validation via bootstrap resampling and permutation testing confirmed significant performance differences between architectures, with large effect sizes between the two newer models and YOLOv5s. A learning curve analysis identified performance saturation at approximately 600–700 training images, providing practical annotation budget guidance for similar binary inspection tasks. These findings are based on a single dataset and validation set of 130 images; independent validation on other casting types and production environments is necessary before broader deployment conclusions can be drawn.

Future work follows a staged trajectory: near-term extensions include multi-view inspection, multi-class defect taxonomy, and adaptive resolution strategies; medium-term development integrates real-time casting process data for predictive quality intervention; and the long-term objective is a federated, self-optimising inspection network enabling closed-loop process control across distributed manufacturing operations.
